accuracy.evidence: Checked against NOAA/NESDIS SciJinks: 5-day forecast right about 90% of the time, 7-day about 80%, 10-day or longer about half; NWS radiosonde fact sheet: balloons launched twice daily from about 900 sites, flights over 2 hours, above 30 km, then burst; Met Office guide: 70% = a 7 in 10 chance of precipitation at that place, not 70% of the time or area; Met Office warnings yellow (be aware), amber (be prepared), red (take action). Radar range is given as 'about 200 km' (NEXRAD precipitation range ~230 km). The radar map keeps 1 square = 10 km and 1 square an hour, so the 9 am to 1 pm arrival is internally consistent.

misconceptions.evidence: Predictions and slips target documented errors: reading a 70% chance as 70% of the day (Met Office Tech Note 665 / Gigerenzer 2005 list both the time and area readings, and the challenge feedback names both), thinking a west wind blows towards the west, expecting a 10-day forecast to be as sure as tomorrow's, using the back edge of the rain instead of the front edge, and confusing which tool maps rain now (balloon vs radar).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfcast is about how a forecast is made: tool-to-job matching for satellite, radar, balloon and station; timing radar rain carried by a west wind; five model runs that agree on day 1 and spread to 12-20 C by day 7; building 70% as 7 rainy days of 10; planning around a yellow wind warning. It shares no scene with flagwxinst (ground instruments and siting), flagwxclim (30-year averages) or flagstorm (lightning), and the lab_distinct gate passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea before the text states it: dragging the rain shows the clock advancing 1 hour per square and the town turning rainy at 1 pm; pressing Run the computer five times shows the grey spread bars widening day by day before the learner picks the surest day; toggling boxes reports n rainy days = n x 10% live; the DONE messages then confirm the rule.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions each have a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'A weather balloon' (the balloon goes to the air job, radar to rain-now), 'Towards the west' (the rain visibly moves east from the 8 am ghost), 'The one for next week' (the runs fan out by day 7), and 'It will rain for 70% of the day' (the 10 boxes are 10 separate days). The reveal line names the learner's pick and the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions with wrong options tagged by slip; fix() gives a specific message for each: tool (which tool does which job), back (time before now), edge (front edge vs back edge with the 3-hour working), pct (time or area reading of a percentage, with 3 in 10 restated), far (errors grow so runs spread), west (winds named for where they come from), warn (yellow, amber, red order). In-scene slips are just as specific, e.g. putting a raincoat on Saturday says Saturday is sunny and Monday has the 90% rain.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK grade 3.2 (limit 6.5) for ages 7-9: short sentences, one idea each, key words meteorologist, radar and satellite defined in place. Adult text FK 9.1 (limit 9.5) with curriculum terms (KS2 working scientifically, NGSS 3-ESS2-1, 3-ESS3-1, radiosonde, ensemble). Canvas labels are 11-15 px bold dark text on light tiles.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler phrases and every kid paragraph carries one mechanism (tools, wind carrying rain with a counting method, model runs, chance and warnings). Step texts give the task in one or two sentences; spoken feedback states the result with numbers (front of the rain is 2 squares from the town; 4 rainy days out of 10 is 40%).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots before, during and after each Show me: job tiles are 2 x 2 with wrapped 12 px text, tool tray tiles stay legible, time keys and the Run the computer key are at least 42 px tall, day labels fit after moving the plot's right edge to 90% (Day 7 was clipped at 95% and fixed), radar time labels moved above the map after they were unreadable on the blob, and the three day cards wrap their forecast text without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: Pick the Satellite then a job, 1 hour on / 1 hour back and the three times, Run the computer again and Day 1-7, Add or Remove a rainy day and Check my 10 days, the three answers, and plan-then-day buttons naming the day's forecast. Each result is spoken through c.say and the canvas aria-label; challenge feedback is in a polite live region and right or wrong is given in words as well as colour. The walk gate's axe run was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: NOAA NESDIS SciJinks, 'How Reliable Are Weather Forecasts?' (5-day ~90%, 7-day ~80%, 10-day+ about half)
NOAA National Weather Service, 'Radiosonde Observation' fact sheet and weather balloon poster (twice daily at 00 and 12 UTC, almost 900 stations, flights over 2 hours, bursts above 30 km)
Met Office, 'What does this forecast mean?' (a 70% chance is a 7 in 10 chance of precipitation at that location) and Tech Note 665 on misreadings of probability of precipitation
Met Office weather warnings guide (yellow: be aware, amber: be prepared, red: take action)
NOAA NWS NEXRAD radar overview (radio waves reflected by precipitation, precipitation range about 230 km)
